title: Learning to Control Anger When a Colleague Takes Credit
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] During yesterday's meeting, my colleague Bram presented an idea as his own, even though I had explained that exact plan to him privately last week.
Narrator: While he was speaking, I felt my chest tighten, and I had to stop myself from interrupting him in front of our entire department.
Narrator: [carefully] Part of me wanted to correct him immediately, loudly enough that everyone would understand what had actually happened between us.
Narrator: However, I remembered something my father once told me: reacting in anger rarely fixes the original problem, it usually just creates a second one.
Narrator: [reflective] So instead of speaking up right there, I stayed quiet, took a few slow breaths, and waited until the meeting had ended completely.
Narrator: Afterward, I asked Bram to speak privately, and even though my hands were still slightly shaking, I kept my voice calm and steady.
Narrator: [honestly] I told him exactly what I had noticed, and I asked him directly why he presented the idea without mentioning where it originally came from.
Narrator: To my surprise, he looked genuinely embarrassed and admitted he had been nervous about the presentation and simply forgot to credit me in the moment.
Narrator: [seriously] I did not fully believe that explanation, yet I decided that assuming the worst about him would only damage our working relationship further.
Narrator: If I had shouted at him during the meeting, he probably would have defended himself instead of actually listening to what I was saying.
Narrator: [gently] Despite still feeling a little hurt, I accepted his apology, and he promised to mention my contribution clearly in the next department update.
Narrator: Controlling my anger did not erase what happened, but it kept the door open for an honest conversation instead of a lasting conflict between us.
Narrator: [encouraging] I am learning that patience under pressure is not weakness; it is choosing a slower, wiser response over a quick, satisfying one.
Narrator: Bram mentioned my idea properly in this morning's update, and honestly, that felt far better than any argument would have.

options: Mistake and misconduct require evidence and different responses

options: A controlled response that still protects credit and accountability
